headline: You build backend changes in careful steps, with tests and escape routes.

archetype.name: The Transaction Guardian
archetype.description: You ask how changes behave under pressure, failure, and rollback. Small steps, explicit tests, and operational documents make your plans reviewable.

dimensions.title: Small Verified Steps
dimensions.summary: You often plan before implementation, narrow the next step, and request tests before changing behavior.

evidence.quote: Good plan. Let's start with step 1 only: the database migration.
Before we refactor the invoice generator, write characterization tests that pin down the current behaviour.

dimensions.title: Concise Explicit Requests
dimensions.summary: You use direct English and specify scope, sequencing, and output formats.

evidence.quote: Write the migration and a rollback. Do not touch the handlers yet.
Turn the checklist into a GitHub issue template.

dimensions.title: Database Close Work
dimensions.summary: Your requests center on Go and PostgreSQL, with concrete choices around concurrency, isolation, and SQL tooling.

evidence.quote: Review this Go function for race conditions. Explain your reasoning step by step.
I want to model double-entry bookkeeping in PostgreSQL. What constraints guarantee that every transaction balances?
Please don't use an ORM here, plain sqlc queries.

dimensions.title: Correctness Meets Operations
dimensions.summary: You repeatedly focus on transactional guarantees, safe rollouts, and evidence that production behavior is observable.

evidence.quote: Add a test that proves the webhook is not written when the transaction rolls back.

dimensions.title: Understand Before Choosing
dimensions.summary: You use explanations and comparisons to explore concurrency and database trade-offs alongside implementation.

evidence.quote: What are the trade-offs between using a mutex here and a channel?
Explain how this behaves under READ COMMITTED versus SERIALIZABLE.

traits.name: Scope Keeper
